cards.explanation: The answer is False. Rezin, king of Aram, and Pekah, king of Israel, march up together to wage war against Jerusalem, but the text says “…he could not overpower the city.” (Isaiah 7:1) That's a whole lot of marching, friends, for a city that still isn't overpowered.

The answer is that their hearts tremble like trees in the wind. When the news reaches the house of David, the hearts of Ahaz, king of Judah, and his people trembled “…like trees in the forest shaken by the wind.” (Isaiah 7:2) A whole forest, getting shaken. I think that's what bad news feels like in the chest.

The answer is False. There's no march in this message, friends. The LORD tells Isaiah the prophet to say to Ahaz, “Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid or disheartened…” (Isaiah 7:4) A shaking king hears about calming down, not gathering troops. That's a whole different kind of plan.

The answer is two smoldering stubs of firewood. That's the LORD's picture of Rezin, king of Aram, and the son of Remaliah, king of Israel. Verse 4 says, “…these two smoldering stubs of firewood…” (Isaiah 7:4) A smoldering stub is barely holding a glow. I think it's a very small thing to lose sleep over.

The answer is the son of Tabeal. That's the name in the plot. Aram and Ephraim say, “Then we can install the son of Tabeal over it as king.” (Isaiah 7:6) The Bible tells us nothing more about him, so I won't make anything up. He's the name on their plan, friends, and that's all we have.

The answer is True. The Lord GOD tells Ahaz, “It will not arise; it will not happen.” (Isaiah 7:7) The two kings made a plan, and the Lord GOD answered it in one short sentence. Their plan doesn't stand a chance.

The word is shattered. God says, “Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered as a people.” (Isaiah 7:8) That's a big word for a big change. And notice God puts a number on it, friends: sixty-five years.

The answer is his faith. God says it plainly to Ahaz: “If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.” (Isaiah 7:9) After all that talk about kings and plots, God lands on faith. That's what He tells Ahaz to stand firm in. And I'd say that's worth writing on the flour jar.

The answer is a sign. The LORD tells Ahaz, “Ask for a sign from the LORD your God…” (Isaiah 7:11) A sign is something Ahaz could see with his own eyes. The LORD is the one inviting him to ask, friends.

The answer is False. Ahaz turns the offer down. The LORD says to ask for a sign, and Ahaz replies, “I will not ask; I will not test the LORD.” (Isaiah 7:12) The text doesn't say why he answers that way, and I won't guess. All we know is he says no to a sign.

Isaiah answers by asking if David's house will try God's patience. He says, “Hear now, O house of David! Is it not enough to try the patience of men? Will you try the patience of my God as well?” (Isaiah 7:13) Isaiah the prophet is speaking to the house of David, which is the family of kings Ahaz belongs to. His answer is two pointed questions, friends.

The answer is the Lord Himself. Isaiah says, “Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign…” (Isaiah 7:14) Ahaz had said, “I will not ask; I will not test the LORD.” (Isaiah 7:12) Ahaz said no to asking, and the Lord Himself gives one anyway.

The answer is True. Isaiah says, “For before the boy knows enough to reject evil and choose good, the land of the two kings you dread will be laid waste.” (Isaiah 7:16) Ahaz has been dreading those two kings, and Isaiah tells him their land will be laid waste. That's a promise with a timeline attached, friends.

The answer is the king of Judah and his people. Isaiah says, “The LORD will bring on you and on your people and on the house of your father a time unlike any since the day Ephraim separated from Judah…” (Isaiah 7:17) Ahaz is the king of Judah, so "you" means him. His people and the house of his father are in it too.

The answer is False. The whistle works, friends. The LORD whistles to the flies at the farthest streams of the Nile and to the bees in Assyria, and “…they will all come and settle…” (Isaiah 7:19) Every last one of them shows up. That's a pretty obedient swarm.

The answer is the beard. The Lord uses the razor “…to shave your head and the hair of your legs, and to remove your beard as well.” (Isaiah 7:20) The razor is the king of Assyria, hired from beyond the Euphrates. It leaves nothing out, friends.

The answer is False. There's plenty, friends. The text says, “…from the abundance of milk they give, he will eat curds…” (Isaiah 7:22) One young cow and two sheep, and still an abundance. The man has plenty to eat.

The answer is all who remain in the land. The text says, “for all who remain in the land will eat curds and honey.” (Isaiah 7:22) The verse doesn't pick favorites. Everyone who remains is at the table.

The answer is briers and thorns. The text says, “…in every place that had a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels of silver, only briers and thorns will be found.” (Isaiah 7:23) Those vines were worth a lot of silver, friends. And now it's only briers and thorns.

The answer is True. The text says, “Men will go there with bow and arrow, for the land will be covered with briers and thorns.” (Isaiah 7:24) Bow and arrow, and briers and thorns everywhere. The land has gone from tended to overgrown.

The answer is places for oxen and sheep. The verse says, “they will become places for oxen to graze and sheep to trample.” (Isaiah 7:25) These are hills once tilled by the hoe, friends. Now it's animals doing the walking.
